title: Towers of Hanoi: A Complete Recursive Visualization
beats: Cold-open clip of the later 'blow your mind' line; presenter admits it took him days to solve and years to understand
Setup: three rods, stacked discs, move one at a time to a destination
The one catch: never a larger disc on a smaller one; this rule is what makes it hard
Three phases: puzzle strategy, recursive program, unravel the recursion with animations
Skip n=1,2 as boring; pause and solve n=3 yourself
Random guessing: three plausible moves lead to a stuck state
Lesson from the failure: largest disc must move first, so top two must be parked on rod 2
Solve n=3 via the subtasks: top two to rod 2, big disc to 3, top two to 3
n=4: pause and try; map it to a 3-disc problem ignoring the biggest disc, destination rod 2
Points out same logic reappeared: this is where recursion originates
Finish n=4; the 2- and 3-disc subproblems recur repeatedly
Hierarchical recap of the n=4 subtasks
Formal statement: hanoi(n,start,end) outputs move list; worked example n=3, 1->3; arrow notation a->b
Write trivial print_move helper first to beat intimidation
Aside: three steps for recursion: base case, recursive leap of faith, build f(n) from f(n-1)
Dominoes analogy mapped step by step; each step's failure shown as a domino that doesn't fall
Apply step 1: base case is print_move(start,end)
Step 2: assume all n-1 calls work for any start/end pair
Need the third rod: other = 6 - start - end
Map puzzle strategy to code: hanoi(n-1,start,other), print_move, hanoi(n-1,other,end)
Pause to appreciate the simplicity; the hook line lands here
Full Python; 'the code basically writes itself'
Trace n=3 call by call, synced to disc animation; returns to the opening example
Encourages working examples yourself to be convinced
Big-picture recap of the three phases and why puzzle-first

new_moves.name: failure-as-constraint-source
new_moves.what: A failed brute-force attempt is mined for the key constraint that drives the real strategy
new_moves.evidence: 2:46-3:26 stuck state reveals the largest disc must go first

new_moves.name: analogy-failure-mapping
new_moves.what: Each step of the framework is justified by showing what breaks in the analogy if that step is missing

new_moves.name: forward-then-unwind
new_moves.what: Teach the abstraction top-down (leap of faith), then separately unwind execution bottom-up for those who distrust it

theory: The video teaches recursion twice in opposite directions: first as a strategy discovered by hand on concrete puzzles where the n-1 subproblem visibly repeats, then as a trusted abstraction (leap of faith), and finally by mechanically unwinding the calls on the same n=3 example. The puzzle phase makes the code feel inevitable ('writes itself'), and the trace answers the residual distrust that the abstraction leaves.
velocity: Orchestrator playbook for recursion: hand-solve n=3, n=4 with sim, then leap-of-faith framework, then call-stack trace on the original n=3.
Scene builder: in the trace, show the subproblem the current call is trying to achieve alongside the global state (16:43).
Learner model: let the learner make the random-guess moves and get stuck; harvest the constraint from their failure rather than stating it.
Voice: when a subproblem recurs, explicitly say 'same as before' — the repetition must be named, not just shown (6:08).
Evals: check that notation appears only after at least two concrete solved examples.
